title: Java Fundamentals
description: The core of the language and the points interviews ask about most, updated for Java 21 (LTS).
resumo: The JVM runs bytecode produced by `javac`, so the same `.class` runs on any system. The JDK brings the compiler and tools; since Java 11 there is no separate JRE.
Primitives (`int`, `double`) hold values; wrappers (`Integer`) are objects and can be null. Compare objects with `equals`, never `==`.
`String` is immutable: building text in a loop creates new objects — use `StringBuilder`.
Checked exceptions require `try/catch` or `throws`; unchecked (`RuntimeException`) signal bugs or broken rules. try-with-resources closes files and connections.
Java is always pass-by-value: a method gets a copy of the value or of the reference.
`List` is the default collection; `List.of()` creates an immutable one.
Modern Java: `var` (10), switch expression (14), text blocks (15), records (16), sealed classes (17).

subsections.subtitle: JVM, JRE and JDK
subsections.description: How Java code goes from source file to running program.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you write code on Windows and the server runs Linux. A program compiled to native machine code would have to be rebuilt for each operating system.

**Concept:** `javac` compiles `.java` files into bytecode (`.class`), which does not depend on the operating system. The JVM runs that bytecode: it loads classes, interprets them, compiles hot code to native code at runtime (the JIT) and manages memory with the garbage collector. JRE = JVM + standard library, enough to run programs. JDK = JRE + development tools (`javac`, `jar`, `jshell`, `jcmd`, debugger).

**How it works:** compile once, run on any JVM. Since Java 11 there is no separate JRE download: you install a JDK, or build a small custom runtime with `jlink`. For a quick test, `java Hello.java` compiles and runs a single file in one step.
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between the JVM, the JRE and the JDK?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Compiling with a newer JDK than the JVM that will run the code. The class file records its version, and an older JVM refuses it. Compile with `--release` set to the oldest Java version you need to support.
examples.code:
$ javac Hello.java              # JDK 21
$ /opt/jdk17/bin/java Hello     # older JVM
UnsupportedClassVersionError: Hello has been compiled by a more recent version
of the Java Runtime (class file version 65.0), this version of the Java Runtime
only recognizes class file versions up to 61.0

# RIGHT: target the oldest JVM that will run the code
$ javac --release 17 Hello.java

subsections.subtitle: Control Flow
subsections.description: Deciding and repeating: if, switch and loops.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** programs constantly decide and repeat: apply a discount only for VIP customers, process every item in a cart.

**Concept:** `if`/`else` decides; `switch` chooses among values; `for`, enhanced `for`, `while` and `do-while` repeat. `break` leaves a loop and `continue` jumps to the next iteration. The switch expression (standard since Java 14) returns a value with `->`, never falls through, and must cover every case.

**How it works:** use the classic `for` when you need the index, the enhanced `for` to walk a collection, and `while` when you do not know in advance how many iterations there will be. Prefer the switch expression for choosing a value: the compiler complains if a case is missing.
examples.interview_question: How does the switch expression improve on the classic switch?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: The classic `switch` with `:` falls through to the next case when you forget `break`, so the code of other cases runs too. The arrow form `->` never falls through.

subsections.subtitle: Primitive Types and Wrappers
subsections.description: int vs Integer, autoboxing and var.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the number 10 can be a raw value or an object. Collections only hold objects, and a database column may be null — a raw `int` cannot be.

**Concept:** Java has 8 primitive types: `byte`, `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `char`, `boolean`. They hold the value directly, are fast and are never null. Each has a wrapper class (`Integer`, `Long`, `Double`, `Boolean`...): an object that can be null and can be used in collections and generics. Autoboxing converts between them automatically.

**How it works:** use primitives for calculations and local values, and wrappers when null is meaningful or a collection requires an object. `var` (Java 10) lets the compiler infer the type of a local variable from its initial value.
examples.code:
int count = 10;                     // primitive: the value itself
Integer boxed = count;              // autoboxing: int -> Integer
int back = boxed;                   // unboxing: Integer -> int
List<Integer> ids = List.of(1, 2);  // collections need wrappers

int parsed = Integer.parseInt("42");
long big = 3_000_000_000L;          // too big for int: long with the L suffix
var name = "Ana";                   // var: inferred as String
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between int and Integer, and why can == fail between two Integer values?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Comparing wrappers with `==` compares objects, not values. It seems to work for small numbers, because -128 to 127 are cached, and fails above that. Unboxing a null wrapper throws `NullPointerException`.
examples.code:
Integer a = 127, b = 127;
System.out.println(a == b);        // true  (cached values -128..127)
Integer c = 1000, d = 1000;
System.out.println(c == d);        // false (different objects)
System.out.println(c.equals(d));   // true  — compare wrappers with equals

Integer stock = null;              // e.g. a nullable database column
int units = stock;                 // NullPointerException on unboxing

subsections.subtitle: Access Modifiers
subsections.description: Controlling who can see and change what.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** if any class can set an account balance directly, nothing guarantees it never goes negative.

**Concept:** Java has four access levels: `private` (only the class itself), no modifier or package-private (classes in the same package), `protected` (same package plus subclasses) and `public` (everyone). Hiding fields and exposing methods that check the rules is encapsulation.

**How it works:** start everything as `private` and open only what other classes really need. Fields stay private; the public methods are the class's contract.
examples.interview_question: What are Java's access modifiers and how do they support encapsulation?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Public fields. Any class can bypass the rules, and the class can no longer change how it stores its data without breaking callers.

subsections.subtitle: The static Keyword
subsections.description: Members that belong to the class, not to each object.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** some things belong to the class, not to each object: a constant such as the tax rate, or a helper method that needs no state.

**Concept:** a `static` member belongs to the class: there is one copy shared by every instance, and it is used without creating an object (`Math.max(3, 7)`). `static final` declares a constant. A static method cannot use `this` or instance fields.

**How it works:** use `static` for constants and for stateless helper methods. Everything that varies per object stays as an instance field.
examples.interview_question: When is static appropriate, and why can mutable static state cause problems?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Mutable static state. It is shared by every request, every thread and every test, so one user's data leaks into another's and tests affect each other. Pass the state as a parameter instead.

subsections.subtitle: Strings and Immutability
subsections.description: Why String never changes, and how to build text.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** text is everywhere — names, messages, JSON — and building it the wrong way creates many throwaway objects.

**Concept:** `String` is immutable: methods such as `toUpperCase()` or `replace()` return a new String and the original never changes. That makes strings safe to share between threads and to use as `HashMap` keys. `StringBuilder` is the mutable version, for building text step by step. Text blocks (Java 15) write multi-line text without escapes.

**How it works:** always use the value a String method returns. In loops, append to a `StringBuilder`; for a single line, `+` is fine — the compiler optimizes it.
examples.interview_question: Why are Strings immutable in Java, and when should you use StringBuilder?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Comparing strings with `==`. It compares references, so text that came from a request, a file or the database is never "the same object". Use `equals`, with the literal on the left to be safe with null.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** files go missing, networks fail, input is invalid. Without handling, one error ends the request with a stack trace.

**Concept:** `throw` signals an error; `try` runs code that may fail; `catch` handles one exception type; `finally` always runs, for cleanup. try-with-resources closes anything `AutoCloseable` — files, connections, streams — automatically, even when an error happens.

**How it works:** catch the most specific type first, and only where you can do something useful; otherwise let the exception propagate. When you wrap an exception in another, pass the original as the cause so the stack trace is kept.
examples.interview_question: What is try-with-resources and when should you use it?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Swallowing exceptions with an empty `catch`, or throwing a new exception without the cause. The error disappears, and the bug shows up later, far from where it happened.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** arrays have a fixed size, but real data grows: cart items, users by id, unique tags.

**Concept:** `List` is ordered, allows duplicates and is accessed by index (`ArrayList`). `Set` has no duplicates (`HashSet`; `LinkedHashSet` keeps insertion order). `Map` associates keys to values (`HashMap`). `List.of`, `Set.of` and `Map.of` create immutable collections.

**How it works:** declare the variable with the interface (`List<String>`) and choose the implementation on the right side. That keeps your code independent of the implementation, which can be changed in one place.
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between List, Set and Map, and when do you use each?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Removing elements from a list while iterating it with a for-each loop throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. Use `removeIf`, or an explicit `Iterator` and its `remove()`.

subsections.subtitle: Arrays
subsections.description: Fixed-size sequences and the Arrays helper class.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** sometimes the number of values is fixed — the 12 months, a grid of pixels — or an API hands you an array, like `main(String[] args)`.

**Concept:** an array has a fixed size set at creation, indexes from 0 to `length - 1`, and elements that start as 0, false or null. Index access is fast, but it cannot grow. The `Arrays` class helps with `sort`, `toString`, `equals` and `asList`.

**How it works:** in business code prefer `List`, which grows and has a richer API. `int[]` is worth it for large amounts of numbers, because `ArrayList<Integer>` stores objects (boxing), not primitives.
examples.interview_question: When is an array better than an ArrayList?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Printing an array or comparing two arrays with `==` or `equals` works on the reference, not the content. Use `Arrays.toString` and `Arrays.equals`. Indexes go up to `length - 1`.
examples.code:
int[] a = {1, 2};
int[] b = {1, 2};
System.out.println(a);                    // [I@1b6d3586 — not the content
System.out.println(a.equals(b));          // false: compares references
System.out.println(Arrays.equals(a, b));  // true: compares content
System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));   // [1, 2]

a[2] = 3;   // ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: the last index is 1

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the same logic copied into several places means every fix has to be made several times.

**Concept:** a method is a named block with parameters and a return type. Overloading is several methods with the same name and different parameter lists. Varargs (`int... values`) accept any number of arguments. Java is always pass-by-value: a primitive argument is a copy of the value; for an object, the reference is copied — the method can change the object, but cannot make the caller's variable point to another object.

**How it works:** keep methods small, with a name that says what they do. To give a new value back to the caller, return it.

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Expecting a method to change the caller's variable. The method receives a copy, so reassigning the parameter has no effect outside. Return the new value instead.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a price that is off by a cent, or a condition that crashes on null — often the cause is the operator, not the logic.

**Concept:** Java has arithmetic (`+ - * / %`), comparison (`== != < >`), logical (`&& || !`), assignment (`+=`), increment (`++`) and ternary (`cond ? a : b`) operators. `* / %` run before `+ -`, and `&&` before `||`. `&&` and `||` short-circuit: the right side runs only if it can change the result.

**How it works:** use parentheses whenever the order is not obvious. Put the null check on the left of `&&`, so the right side never runs on null.
examples.interview_question: What are short-circuit operators, and what goes wrong with 1 / 3 in Java?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Integer division and `double` for money. `int / int` throws the decimals away, and `double` cannot represent values such as 0.1 exactly. Cast before dividing, and use `BigDecimal` for money.
examples.code:
int done = 1, total = 3;
double ratio = done / total;          // 0.0: int / int discards the decimals
double ok = (double) done / total;    // 0.333...

System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);        // 0.30000000000000004
BigDecimal sum = new BigDecimal("0.1").add(new BigDecimal("0.2"));   // 0.3

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** `Car` and `Motorcycle` share a brand, a year and `describe()`. Copying them into each class duplicates the code and every fix.

**Concept:** `extends` makes a class inherit the fields and methods of another (a class has only one parent). The subclass can add members and override methods (`@Override`). `super` calls the parent's constructor or method. A `final` class cannot be extended; a `sealed` class (Java 17) lists exactly which classes may extend it.

**How it works:** the subclass constructor calls `super(...)` first. When a method is called, the object's real type decides which version runs — that is polymorphism.
examples.interview_question: How does inheritance work in Java, and what does super do?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Inheriting only to reuse code when the subclass is not really a kind of the parent. A stack that extends `ArrayList` also inherits `add(index, item)`, and callers can break the stack rule. Use a field instead (composition).

subsections.subtitle: Optional
subsections.description: Saying in the return type that a value may be missing.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** `findByEmail` may find nothing. Returning `null` relies on every caller remembering a null check — one forgets, and there is a `NullPointerException`.

**Concept:** `Optional<T>` is a box that is either empty or holds one value, and the return type tells the caller "this may be missing". Its methods handle both cases: `map`, `filter`, `orElse`, `orElseGet`, `orElseThrow`, `ifPresent`.

**How it works:** use it as the return type of methods that may not find something. Do not use it for fields, parameters or collections — for collections, return an empty list.
examples.interview_question: How does Optional improve on returning null, and where should you not use it?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Calling `get()` without checking, which throws on an empty Optional — the same problem as null. Also, `orElse(...)` always evaluates its argument, even when a value is present; for an expensive fallback use `orElseGet`.

subsections.subtitle: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions
subsections.description: When the compiler forces you to handle an error.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** some failures are expected and recoverable, like a missing file; others are bugs, like dereferencing null. Java separates them so the compiler can make you deal with the first kind.

**Concept:** checked exceptions are subclasses of `Exception` other than `RuntimeException` (`IOException`, `SQLException`): the compiler requires `try`/`catch` or `throws`. Unchecked exceptions are `RuntimeException` and its subclasses (`NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`), with no such requirement. `Error` (`OutOfMemoryError`) means a JVM problem and should not be caught.

**How it works:** modern Spring code uses unchecked domain exceptions, such as `OrderNotFoundException`, handled in one central place (`@RestControllerAdvice`) instead of `throws` in every layer. When you cannot recover from a checked exception, wrap it in an unchecked one, keeping the cause.
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions, and when do you create each?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: `catch (Exception e)` everywhere. It also catches bugs such as `NullPointerException`, which then fail silently. Catch only the exceptions you expect and can handle.

subsections.subtitle: equals() and hashCode()
subsections.description: The contract that makes HashMap and HashSet work.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** two `Email` objects hold the same address, yet a `Set` treats them as different and stores both.

**Concept:** `==` compares references; `equals` compares content — but the default `equals` in `Object` is just `==`, so value classes must override it. The contract: equal objects must have the same `hashCode`. `HashMap` and `HashSet` first use `hashCode` to pick a bucket, then `equals` inside that bucket.

**How it works:** override both, using the same fields, with `Objects.equals` and `Objects.hash`. For value objects, prefer records, which generate both from all their components.
examples.interview_question: What happens if you override equals() but not hashCode()?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Overriding only `equals`. Two equal objects get different hash codes, land in different buckets, and the `Set` or `Map` cannot find them. Changing a field used by `hashCode` after the object is in a `HashSet` causes the same problem.

subsections.subtitle: Dates with java.time
subsections.description: The modern, immutable date and time API.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** due dates, delivery deadlines, users in different time zones. The old `Date` and `Calendar` are mutable, start months at 0, and mix up "a date" with "a moment".

**Concept:** `java.time` (Java 8+) is immutable and thread-safe, with one class per idea: `LocalDate` (a date, no time zone), `LocalDateTime` (date and time, no zone), `ZonedDateTime` and `OffsetDateTime` (with a zone or offset), `Instant` (a moment on the UTC timeline), `Duration` and `Period` (amounts of time).

**How it works:** store moments as `Instant` (or `OffsetDateTime`) and convert to the user's time zone only to display them. Use `LocalDate` for things that really have no time, like a birthday.
examples.interview_question: Why use java.time instead of Date and Calendar?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Using `LocalDateTime` for events. It has no zone, so "10:00" could be any city, and servers in another zone shift it. Store the moment, and convert it only for display.
